It was developed by experts from the Global Hepatitis Programme and reviewed by scientific committee members from WHO's six regions. The guidelines aim to provide technical approaches for acute hepatitis surveillance, focusing on enhanced case reporting and differentiation between acute and chronic hepatitis. Acute viral hepatitis surveillance is critical for understanding new infections, identifying risk factors, and tracking progress toward elimination. WHO recommends monitoring acute hepatitis cases to gather data on new infections, chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) prevalence, and mortality from complications like cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Acute hepatitis surveillance traditionally operates within communicable disease systems, but most new HBV and HCV infections are asymptomatic, making diagnosis challenging. Enhanced case reporting captures symptomatic cases, providing valuable insights into new infections and trends. Acute hepatitis can result from new infections or flares of chronic HBV. Surveillance systems must differentiate between these to ensure specificity. WHO has developed standardized case definitions combining clinical symptoms and biomarker criteria to exclude chronic infections. Syndromic surveillance and enhanced case reporting are complementary approaches, with syndromic surveillance focusing on outbreak detection and enhanced reporting providing detailed data on trends and risk factors. Enhanced case reporting requires significant resources, including public health infrastructure and trained personnel. It is more feasible in high-income countries, where systems like the United States' Viral Hepatitis Surveillance Program collect nationwide data on serologically confirmed acute hepatitis cases. Sentinel surveillance sites in lowand middle-income countries can also implement enhanced reporting, focusing on acute hepatitis cases in community settings. The guidelines outline criteria for selecting sentinel sites, emphasizing the need for in-vitro diagnostic capacity, access to acute hepatitis patients, and human resources for case investigations. Surveillance should target healthcare facilities where most acute hepatitis cases are likely to present. Data collection involves in-vitro diagnosis, biomarker testing, and risk factor assessment using standardized questionnaires. Sampling strategies aim to capture all eligible cases, with sample size considerations ensuring sufficient statistical power for analysis. Testing strategies for acute hepatitis cases include simultaneous testing for all biomarkers of recent infection or stepwise testing based on clinical and epidemiological criteria. These approaches aim to identify recent infections and inform public health interventions. Sentinel surveillance systems should be institutionalized for long-term implementation, with data aggregated across sites to enhance analysis and interpretation.
